newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Inkatha implicated in S.African hit-squad murders.
newsitem.headline: Inkatha implicated in S.African hit-squad murders.

text.p: The leader of a band of hit-squad killers told South Africa's truth body on Tuesday that orders for the murder of political opponents came from the right-hand man of Zulu leader Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi.
Daluxolo Luthuli, the political commissar of some 200 Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) men given military training by the former white state, also alleged Buthelezi knew of the killings.
The IFP leaders denied his claims.

"I am instructed by my clients, Mr. Khumalo and the president of the IFP, Dr Buthelezi, that they vehemently deny these allegations and that there is no truth in them," lawyer Patrick Falconer told Reuters.
Luthuli said there were so many murders ordered by him and Buthelezi's personal assistant Zakhele Khumalo that he could not remember the exact number or names of all the victims.

"I was still their (the trainees') political commissar and I gave them a lot of orders, especially about the killing of United Democratic Front members. The instructions came directly from the IFP," he told the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. "They always came from myself or Mr Khumalo."
Asked by reporters after the hearing whether Buthelezi knew of the killings, Luthuli said: "Definitely, without a doubt, the president of the IFP knew of all these things."

Khumalo was last year acquitted on 13 murder charges stemming from his role as a link between the trainees and the military. The murders were the result of a hit-squad attack on a family near the east coast city of Durban in 1987.

Luthuli charged that the trainees, who received government- sanctioned instruction from Military Intelligence in Namibia's Caprivi Strip in 1986, were also involved in assassinating high-profile leaders of now president Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) in the 1990s.
These included the yet-to-be-solved 1992 murder of ANC leader Reggie Radebe who was ambushed while returning from a peace meeting.
Buthelezi, now Mandela's fiercest black political opponent, was the chief minister of the semi-autonomous black homeland government as well as the minister of police.

Buthelezi approached the minority white government in the mid-1980s for military assistance after death threats were made by the then-banned ANC and its allies, including the United Democratic Front, on his life and those of his followers.
One trainee, Gcina Mkhize, told the commission on Tuesday that the trainees were aware that they would be acting illegally once they were deployed across KwaZulu-Natal province.
"We were trained to run away from the police. We were told the things we were trained to do were not lawful in the country," Mkhize said.
The conflict that has raged between Inkatha and the ANC has caused the deaths of over 15,000 people in well over a decade of bitter turf wars in KwaZulu-Natal.
